meta.title: Old English Level 1
meta.subtitle: The 500 commonest words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Old English → English (see the Old English, recall the meaning) and English → Old English (see an English meaning, recall the Old English). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 500 words: the 500 commonest words of Old English prose. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: Old English has no examination and no graded word list, so a level here is a band of frequency, not a stage of conversation. The words were counted over about 112,000 words of Old English prose — Ælfric's Catholic Homilies (Thorpe's 1844 edition), the reading texts of Sweet's Anglo-Saxon Primer and Tatoeba's Old English sentences — by the WHOLE word, every form of a noun or a verb added together, and the cards are dealt in that order, the commonest first. Ælfric was a preacher and most surviving prose is religious, so God, Christ, heaven and the apostles come early; the vocabulary of the poetry is not here. Every headword is printed as modern editions and Wiktionary print it: a macron marks a long vowel (stān, 'stone') and a dot marks ċ and ġ where they are said 'ch' and 'y' (iċ, ġēar), with a reconstructed pronunciation in IPA beneath; the Old English Alphabet deck, the first in this collection, teaches how to read both. There is no speaker, because no voice reads Old English. The 192 nouns show their gender, genitive and plural; the 136 verbs show their class and their principal parts — past, past plural, past participle — which is how a strong verb is learnt; the All forms fold holds the paradigm. 225 of the 500 words show their Modern English descendant where one survives (cyning → king), labelled as a descendant, not a translation. Real example sentences come with 196 of the 500 words, three apiece for 115 of them, the word picked out in colour. Sources. Meanings, gender, class, forms, pronunciation and descendants: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: counted by this deck's generator over B. Thorpe (ed.), The Homilies of the Anglo-Saxon Church, vol. 1 (1844) and H. Sweet, An Anglo-Saxon Primer, 8th ed. (1905), both public domain via Project Gutenberg, and Tatoeba. Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
